morphology.summary: An organelle, not a cell: the largest organelle in most eukaryotic cells, it is bounded by a DOUBLE membrane (the nuclear envelope, two separate lipid bilayers with a perinuclear space between them), perforated by thousands of octagonal nuclear pore complexes. Inside sits the genome as chromatin (denser heterochromatin toward the periphery, looser euchromatin centrally) and the nucleolus, a membrane-less body where ribosomal RNA is transcribed and ribosome subunits are assembled. The outer nuclear membrane is directly continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum and, like it, is studded with ribosomes; the perinuclear space is continuous with the ER lumen. This is the archive and control room of the cell: DNA never leaves it, only working RNA copies do, exported through the pores.
morphology.kind: membrane-bound organelle of eukaryotic cells (absent from bacteria and archaea, which instead have an unbound nucleoid)
morphology.size: Roughly spherical to ellipsoid, about 6 micrometres across in a typical human cell (matches the atlas scale entry: 6 um, ~300 pg dry mass), occupying some 10% of total cell volume - the largest organelle. The perinuclear space between the two envelope membranes is narrow, about 20-50 nm. Each nuclear pore complex is one of the largest macromolecular machines in the cell: roughly 100-120 nm in outer diameter, ~50-60 MDa (up to ~110-125 MDa in vertebrates), built from about 30 different nucleoporin proteins present in multiples of 8 (giving its eight-fold, octagonal symmetry). A typical vertebrate somatic-cell nucleus carries on the order of 2,000-4,000 pore complexes (more in transcriptionally very active cells), i.e. genuinely thousands, scattered fairly evenly over the envelope surface.
morphology.shape: A smooth-surfaced, gently rounded sac (sphere/ellipsoid), its outline interrupted only by the many circular pore openings. In cutaway/section it reads as two closely-spaced parallel lines (the two membranes) enclosing a thin bright gap (the perinuclear space), occasionally bulging outward and pinching into a neat continuity with a ribosome-studded rough-ER cisterna at one or more points on its surface. The interior is filled with a granular-to-fibrous meshwork of chromatin of two densities, plus one or more dense round nucleolar bodies.
morphology.number_per_cell: Almost always exactly one per cell (the defining feature of a eukaryotic somatic cell). Exceptions exist at both extremes and are worth knowing but NOT what a generic teaching image should show: mature mammalian red blood cells and cornified skin cells have none; skeletal muscle fibres and osteoclasts are multinucleate; hepatocytes are often binucleate. A teaching image should show ONE nucleus.
morphology.position_in_cell: Usually roughly central in the cell, though position varies by cell type (e.g. pushed to one edge in a fat cell laden with a lipid droplet). The outer nuclear membrane merges directly into the rough endoplasmic reticulum, which typically radiates outward from one or more points on the nuclear surface, so the nucleus should not be drawn as an isolated bag floating in empty cytoplasm - a patch of ribosome-studded ER continuous with the envelope belongs in the same frame.
morphology.envelope_structure: The nuclear envelope is TWO separate, concentric lipid bilayers, not one: an inner nuclear membrane (INM) facing the nucleoplasm, and an outer nuclear membrane (ONM) facing the cytoplasm, separated by the perinuclear space (~20-50 nm, continuous with the ER lumen). The two membranes are chemically distinct (different resident proteins) but are physically CONTINUOUS with each other at the rim of every nuclear pore, where INM and ONM fuse to form the curved 'pore membrane'. The ONM is studded with ribosomes and is texturally/functionally just an extension of the rough ER; the INM is smooth and lined on its nucleoplasmic face by the nuclear lamina. Drawing the envelope as a single membrane line is THE most common and most serious error for this organelle.
morphology.nuclear_pore_complex: A roughly octagonal (eight-fold symmetric) protein ring assembly seated in the fused pore membrane where INM and ONM meet, built from ~30 different nucleoporin proteins. Functions as the sole gateway for regulated traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm: mRNA, tRNA and ribosomal subunits exit; histones, DNA/RNA polymerases and other nuclear proteins are imported; small molecules diffuse freely, but large cargo needs an active, signal-dependent transport cycle. In face-on (freeze-fracture) view it reads as a ring of eight subunits around a central channel; in cross-section it reads as a gap/channel spanning both membranes where their profiles curve together and fuse.
morphology.chromatin_and_nucleolus: Chromatin (DNA + histone/non-histone proteins) fills the nuclear interior in two visually and functionally distinct states: HETEROCHROMATIN is densely packed, transcriptionally silent, electron-dense (reads dark in TEM), and characteristically hugs the nuclear periphery just inside the lamina (and rims the nucleolus), because it associates with lamin/LBR-based tethers at the inner membrane. EUCHROMATIN is loosely packed, transcriptionally active, electron-lucent (reads pale/open in TEM), and fills the nuclear interior and the zone right around nuclear pores, where exported transcripts have easy access to the pore channels. The NUCLEOLUS is a large (roughly 1-3 um), rounded, membrane-LESS body inside the nucleus, denser and more uniform than the surrounding chromatin, organized internally into a fibrillar centre, dense fibrillar component and granular component; it is where rRNA genes are transcribed and processed and where ribosomal subunits are assembled before export through the pores. It has no boundary of its own - it is a condensation within the nucleoplasm, not a walled-off compartment.
morphology.nuclear_lamina: A thin (~10-30 nm), dense meshwork of lamin intermediate filaments lining the nucleoplasmic face of the inner membrane. Provides mechanical support to the envelope, anchors nuclear pore complexes in the membrane, and tethers peripheral heterochromatin, which is why heterochromatin concentrates right at the envelope.
morphology.colour_note: Like any single organelle, the nucleus is essentially colourless/transparent in life; the blues/purples of stained slides and the vivid tones of coloured EM plates are added convention, not the organelle's real colour. All colour in the teaching images below is convention, chosen for legibility and consistency across styles.

structures.note: THE structure to get right: TWO concentric membranes (inner + outer), not one. Must be drawn as two distinct parallel lines/shells with a visible gap between them, everywhere around the nucleus, including at the point where it meets the ER.
Faces the cytoplasm, studded with ribosomes like rough ER, and is directly continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum - show it flowing into an ER cisterna at at least one point.
Faces the nucleoplasm, smooth (no ribosomes), lined on its inner face by the nuclear lamina.

structures.en: Perinuclear space (gap between the two membranes)
structures.note: The narrow lumen between inner and outer membrane, continuous with the rough ER lumen. Draw as a thin bright/pale gap separating the two membrane lines.

An octagonal (eight-sided) protein ring where the inner and outer membranes fuse into a single continuous pore membrane. Draw MANY (thousands, stippled evenly over the whole envelope surface, not just a handful) - never as simple round holes with no ring structure, and never concentrated in one patch.
A thin dense fibrous sheet just inside the inner membrane. In a cutaway, show it as a fine mesh/line hugging the inside of the inner membrane, with heterochromatin gathered against it.
The ground substance inside the envelope in which chromatin and the nucleolus sit.
Densely packed, dark/electron-dense clumps concentrated at the nuclear periphery against the lamina, and rimming the nucleolus. Transcriptionally silent.

Loosely dispersed, paler, filling the nuclear interior and the zone around nuclear pores. Transcriptionally active. Never draw chromatin as condensed X-shaped chromosomes - that form exists only during mitosis, when the envelope has broken down.

One (occasionally more) dense, rounded body inside the nucleus, denser/more uniform than the surrounding chromatin. It has NO membrane of its own - do not outline it with a boundary line, just render it as a denser texture/colour condensation. Site of rRNA synthesis and ribosome assembly.

structures.la: reticulum endoplasmicum granulosum (continuum cum involucro nucleari)
structures.en: Rough endoplasmic reticulum, continuous with the outer membrane
structures.de: Raues endoplasmatisches Retikulum, im Übergang zur äußeren Kernmembran
structures.note: The single most commonly missed teaching point: the nuclear envelope is not a separate sealed bag. Show a ribosome-studded ER cisterna running off the outer membrane at one or more points on the nuclear surface, with the two membranes of the envelope and the ER's own membrane pair clearly the same structure in continuity.
Context only, filling the frame around the nucleus; may include free ribosomes and a hint of other organelles, but the nucleus should dominate the composition.

do_not_draw: Do NOT draw the nuclear envelope as a SINGLE membrane line. It is a double membrane (inner + outer, with a perinuclear space between them) everywhere around the nucleus - this is the single most important thing to get right and the most common error to avoid.
Do NOT give the nucleolus a membrane or an outline of its own. It has none; render it as a denser, more uniform patch/texture floating in the nucleoplasm, not a walled compartment.

Do NOT draw condensed, X-shaped (metaphase) chromosomes inside an otherwise intact nucleus. That form only exists during mitosis, by which point the nuclear envelope has broken down. Interphase chromatin is a diffuse fibrous/granular mass (denser heterochromatin at the rim, looser euchromatin centrally), never distinct paired-chromatid X shapes.

Do NOT draw a bacterial nucleoid (a naked loop of DNA with no envelope, sitting in a cell that also has a cell wall/capsule/flagella). The nucleus is a membrane-bound eukaryotic organelle; prokaryotes have no true nucleus.
Do NOT draw a plant cell wall or chloroplast around the nucleus. This is a generic eukaryotic organelle plate, not a plant-cell diagram.

Do NOT draw the nucleus as a sealed, isolated bag floating with empty space around it. Its outer membrane is continuous with the rough ER - at least one patch of ribosome-studded ER should be shown merging into the envelope.

Do NOT draw the nuclear pores as simple round holes with no ring structure, and do not draw only a handful of them. There are thousands, each an octagonal protein ring, evenly scattered over the whole surface.

Do NOT anthropomorphise the nucleus itself in the SEM/textbook/3d/watercolor renders (no face, no eyes, no limbs) - that treatment is reserved separately for the coloring-book style only, per project convention.
Do NOT add text, letters, numbers, scale bars, arrows-with-labels or watermarks baked into the image.

colour_legend.nuclear_envelope: outer membrane #6B8CB8 (cool blue-grey), inner membrane #4C6E9E (deeper blue) - two distinct but related blues so the double structure reads clearly
colour_legend.perinuclear_space: #EAF1FA (very pale blue-white slit between the two membrane lines)
colour_legend.nuclear_pore_complex: #F2B441 (warm amber rings), consistent with the amber used for entry/exit gateways in other organelle plates of this atlas
colour_legend.nuclear_lamina: #3A4E70 (dark navy fine mesh, just inside the inner membrane)
colour_legend.heterochromatin: #7B4B8A (deep dusty purple, dense clumps at the periphery and around the nucleolus)
colour_legend.nucleolus: #D9622B (warm terracotta-orange, dense rounded body, no outline of its own)
colour_legend.rough_er_continuity: #9AA7B5 (cool grey-blue sheets with dark ribosome dots, matching the ER convention used for the Golgi-apparatus plate in this same set)
colour_legend.cytosol_context: #EDE7DC (neutral warm grey-beige, softly out of focus)
colour_legend.note: The nucleus has no colour in life and TEM is greyscale; every colour here is teaching convention. The palette's job is to make the double envelope, the pore ring, and the heterochromatin/euchromatin contrast legible at a glance, and it echoes the ER tone already used for the Golgi apparatus plate so the two organelle images sit together as one set.

sources.title: Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell - 'The Transport of Molecules between the Nucleus and the Cytosol' (NCBI Bookshelf NBK26932)
sources.note: Canonical account of the nuclear envelope as two concentric membranes penetrated by nuclear pore complexes, with the inner and outer membranes continuous with each other at the pores yet carrying distinct protein compositions; nuclear import/export of RNAs and nuclear proteins through the pores.

sources.title: Cooper, The Cell: A Molecular Approach - 'The Nuclear Envelope and Traffic between the Nucleus and Cytoplasm' (NCBI Bookshelf NBK9927)
sources.note: States that the outer nuclear membrane is continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum and, like the rough ER, is studded with ribosomes; proteins made on outer-membrane ribosomes are translocated into the perinuclear space, which is continuous with the ER lumen; nuclear pore complexes are the sole channels for nucleocytoplasmic exchange.

sources.title: Cooper, The Cell: A Molecular Approach - 'The Nucleolus' (NCBI Bookshelf NBK9939)
sources.note: Confirms the nucleolus is not surrounded by a membrane and is organised around the chromosomal regions carrying the rRNA genes (nucleolar organizer regions); site of rRNA transcription/processing and ribosome-subunit assembly.

sources.title: Feric et al. and related reviews - nucleolar tripartite structure (summarised via PMC review 'New insights into nucleolar structure and function', PMC4447046) and PMC12071546 'The Nucleolus: A Central Hub for Ribosome Biogenesis'
sources.note: Electron microscopy shows the interphase nucleolus organised into fibrillar centre, dense fibrillar component and granular component; membrane-less, phase-separated body responsible for ribosome biogenesis.

sources.title: Beck & Hurt, 'The nuclear pore complex: understanding its function through structural insight', Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol 18:73 (2017) (context via PMC9100368 'The Nuclear Pore Complex: Birth, Life, and Death of a Cellular Behemoth')
sources.note: NPC as one of the largest macromolecular machines in the cell, mass on the order of 60-125 MDa, eight-fold rotational symmetry built from ~30 different nucleoporins present in multiples of eight, giving the characteristic octagonal ring.

sources.title: Ori et al./general cell-biology reviews on NPC density - summarised via Nature Scientific Reports 'Quantifying Nucleoporin Stoichiometry Inside Single Nuclear Pore Complexes In vivo' (PMC4894440) and standard cell-biology figures
sources.note: Supports the order-of-magnitude figure of roughly 2,000-4,000 nuclear pore complexes in a typical vertebrate somatic-cell envelope (varies with transcriptional activity), i.e. genuinely thousands distributed over the whole surface.

sources.title: Zheng & Guttman group and standard texts on chromatin radial organisation - summarised via PMC7102895 'Positioning heterochromatin at the nuclear periphery suppresses histone turnover to promote epigenetic inheritance' and related TEM chromatin-density literature
sources.note: Confirms the classic radial pattern: heterochromatin enriched at the nuclear periphery and around the nucleolus, euchromatin in the nuclear interior and around nuclear pores; heterochromatin is markedly more electron-dense in TEM due to its higher packing density.

sources.title: Gerace & Blobel; Aebi et al., 'The nuclear lamina is a meshwork of intermediate-type filaments', Nature 323:560 (1986); reviewed via PMC3027047 'Mapping of protein- and chromatin-interactions at the nuclear lamina'
sources.note: Establishes the nuclear lamina as a meshwork of lamin intermediate filaments lining the inner nuclear membrane, providing structural support and an anchoring site for peripheral heterochromatin.

sources.title: OpenStax Biology 2e, 4.3 'Eukaryotic Cells'
sources.note: General teaching-level confirmation of nucleus/nuclear envelope/nucleolus/chromatin terminology and the double-membrane, pore-perforated envelope model used for an introductory audience check.

sources.title: Wikipedia - Cell nucleus / Nuclear envelope / Nuclear pore / Nucleolus (en)
sources.note: Cross-check for the ~6 um typical diameter, ~10% of cell volume, one nucleoplasmic body per cell as the norm, and the exceptions (anucleate erythrocytes, multinucleate skeletal muscle fibres) already referenced in the atlas's own func/deps text.

sources.title: Wikipedia (de) - Zellkern / Kernhülle / Kernpore / Nukleolus
sources.note: German terminology check: Zellkern/Nukleus, Kernhülle (äußere/innere Kernmembran), perinukleärer Raum, Kernporenkomplex, Kernlamina, Chromatin (Heterochromatin/Euchromatin), Nukleoplasma, Nukleolus.

sources.title: Terminologia Histologica (FIPAT/IFAA)
sources.note: Basis for the Latin terms used: nucleus, involucrum nucleare, membrana nuclearis externa/interna, spatium perinucleare, complexus pori nuclearis, lamina nuclearis, nucleoplasma, chromatinum/heterochromatinum/euchromatinum, nucleolus.

reference_micrograph_candidates.title: Pancreatic acinar cells - TEM
reference_micrograph_candidates.attribution: Louisa Howard, Rippel Electron Microscope Facility, Dartmouth College (via Wikimedia Commons). JEOL 100CX TEM.
reference_micrograph_candidates.note: CHOSEN. A large, roughly kidney-shaped nucleus fills the left/centre of the frame with the envelope clearly outlined and a beautiful, textbook-clear pattern of dark heterochromatin clumps against paler euchromatin. Its most valuable feature for THIS organelle: dense, ribosome-studded rough ER sheets crowd the cytoplasm on the upper-right and lower-left and visibly run up to and merge with the nuclear envelope, making the ER-envelope continuity - the single most commonly missed teaching point - directly visible in a real micrograph, not just asserted. 640x480 native, public-domain, same trusted source already used for this set's Golgi-apparatus plate. Trade-off: at this magnification the two envelope membranes are not individually resolved as separate lines (they read as one contour) and no nucleolus is in frame; both points are noted honestly in the render log, and the labelled/illustrated styles carry those details explicitly.
